g.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to
evaluate non-verifiable tasks (Gu et al., 2025; Shao et al.,
2025), particularly for agentic systems in web navigation and tool
use (Chen et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Pan et…
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=6) Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to evaluate non-verifiable tasks (Gu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025), particularly for agentic systems in web navigation and tool use (Chen et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024).

g.text: judges receive trajectory + CoT, assume faithful
In this LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, judges are provided with the agent's
execution trajectory, including observations, actions, and chain-of-thought
(CoT; Xue et al., 2025; Lù et al., 2025)—assuming the CoT faithfully
g.title: N2 [Prior_Work] (cites=4) In this LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, judges are provided with the agent's execution trajectory, including observations, actions, and chain-of-thought (CoT; Xue et al., 2025; Lù et al., 2025)—assuming the CoT faithfully represents the agent's reasoning and improves judgment accuracy (Korbak et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025).

g.text: However, LLM judges exhibit systematic biases, including sensitivity to
surface-level cues, length, and order (Zhao et al., 2025; Huang et al.,
2025; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024).
g.title: N3 [Limitation] (cites=4) However, LLM judges exhibit systematic biases, including sensitivity to surface-level cues, length, and order (Zhao et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024).

g.text: Moreover, LLM-generated CoTs do not always reflect the model's true
reasoning and can function as post-hoc rationalizations (Lanham et al.,
2023; Turpin et al., 2023; Arcuschin et al., 2025).
g.title: N4 [Limitation] (cites=3) Moreover, LLM-generated CoTs do not always reflect the model's true reasoning and can function as post-hoc rationalizations (Lanham et al., 2023; Turpin et al., 2023; Arcuschin et al., 2025).

g.text: Models may also learn to hide misbehavior from the CoT or behave differently
under alignment evaluation (Baker et al., 2025; Schoen et al., 2025).
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=2) Models may also learn to hide misbehavior from the CoT or behave differently under alignment evaluation (Baker et al., 2025; Schoen et al., 2025).

g.text: While these issues have largely been studied in isolation, their combination
gives rise to a particularly concerning failure mode for modern evaluation
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) While these issues have largely been studied in isolation, their combination gives rise to a particularly concerning failure mode for modern evaluation pipelines.

g.text: RQ: can CoT-only manipulation bias judge?
Particularly, we inquire: Can an agent systematically bias an LLM
judge into predicting success—even when the task was not
g.title: N7 [Context: RQ] (cites=0) Particularly, we inquire: Can an agent systematically bias an LLM judge into predicting success—even when the task was not completed—by manipulating only its chain-of-thought?

g.text: This question targets a central assumption underlying LLM-based evaluation
of agents: that exposing the agent's reasoning improves reliability.
g.title: N8 [Context] (cites=0) This question targets a central assumption underlying LLM-based evaluation of agents: that exposing the agent's reasoning improves reliability.

g.text: if assumption fails: rewards presentation not execution

reasoning is presented rather than for whether they actually complete the
g.title: N9 [Context] (cites=0) If this assumption fails, evaluation systems may reward agents for how their reasoning is presented rather than for whether they actually complete the given task.

g.text: In other words, if a judge relies on the agent's CoT more than the actual
actions and environment states, then reasoning traces that exaggerate
progress, obscure failures, or reframe objectives may systematically bias
g.title: N10 [Context] (cites=0) In other words, if a judge relies on the agent's CoT more than the actual actions and environment states, then reasoning traces that exaggerate progress, obscure failures, or reframe objectives may systematically bias evaluation.

g.text: An agent can improve its perceived performance by optimizing how its CoT is
worded, rather than by improving task execution itself.
g.title: N11 [Context] (cites=0) An agent can improve its perceived performance by optimizing how its CoT is worded, rather than by improving task execution itself.

g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) In this paper, we demonstrate that this failure mode is both real and severe.

g.title: N13 [Method] (cites=0) By modifying only the agent's CoT—while keeping actions and environment states fixed—we substantially bias LLM judges toward predicting success (see Fig. 1).

g.text: We explore mitigation strategies, including warning judges not to trust
agent reasoning, judge-time scaling (Khalifa et al., 2025), and rubric-based
methods (Xue et al., 2025), but find that none fully resolve the issue.
